metric.dependency_simplicity.description: TypeScript is a compile-to-JS language whose language-level dependency surface is inherently split across two runtime layers: the TS compiler (tsc) itself plus a mandatory JS execution host (Node.js, browser, or other JS engine). Language-level dependency semantics (import/export, ES module resolution) are simple and standardized, but a working program almost always requires: (1) a package manager manifest (package.json), (2) a tsconfig.json controlling compilation targets/module resolution which has historically been a significant source of configuration complexity (moduleResolution, target, lib settings), and (3) type declaration files (@types/*) for any JS dependency lacking native typings, an extra indirection layer not present in languages with unified toolchains. Reviewed template micro-benchmarks (mb00-mb11) and adversarial programs use only standard ECMAScript imports and no exotic native bindings, indicating the assigned corpus itself has low incidental dependency complexity, which is favorable. However this reflects the workload authors' restraint, not a language-level guarantee: TypeScript's own type system depends on structural typing plus a large ecosystem of ambient .d.ts declaration merging that adds indirect complexity for any non-trivial external dependency graph.
metric.dependency_simplicity.normalization_rule: 0-100 scale, 100 = simplest (no external deps, single toolchain, no runtime host needed); deductions applied for: (a) mandatory separate JS runtime host beyond the compiler (-15), (b) tsconfig.json configuration surface required for real projects (-10), (c) reliance on @types/* ambient declaration ecosystem for non-TS deps (-13).
metric.dependency_simplicity.observation: None of the readable micro-benchmark files exhibited unusual external dependency declarations; they are self-contained scripts compilable with a bare tsc invocation, consistent with the language's ability to run dependency-free for simple programs. This supports a moderate-to-good score, but the two-tier (compiler + runtime host) requirement and the .d.ts/type-declaration indirection layer are structural, language-level dependency-simplicity costs relative to single-binary compiled languages, hence a mid-range normalized score rather than a top score.

metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.description: TypeScript's language design compiles to plain JavaScript (typically ES-standard targets), which is one of the most platform-neutral compilation targets available: the emitted code runs unmodified across browsers, Node.js, Deno, Bun, embedded JS engines, and any ECMAScript-conformant host, with no native code generation, no platform-specific ABI, and no OS-level linking step. The type system is fully erased at compile time (no runtime type-tag dependency), so the emitted artifact carries no platform-specific residue. This is a strong language-level portability design: source is target-triple-independent, and the compiler itself (tsc) runs anywhere Node.js runs.
metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.normalization_rule: 0-100 scale, 100 = fully platform-neutral compiled artifact (portable bytecode/text with no ABI/OS coupling). TypeScript scores high because emitted JS has no native ABI and runs on any conformant engine; deduction applied only for reliance on a JS engine as an intermediary runtime layer rather than direct native execution (-22), which is a language-design characteristic distinct from ecosystem-level platform support breadth (scored elsewhere).
metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.observation: Reviewed micro-benchmark sources use only standard language constructs (arithmetic, control flow, arrays/objects) with no platform-specific APIs (no direct filesystem/OS syscalls, no native FFI), consistent with fully portable, host-neutral TypeScript/JavaScript semantics as authored.
